claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by intrinsically high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy enables easy activation of multiple slip systems.
High stacking-fault energy promotes rapid dislocation cross-slip.
Rapid cross-slip inhibits dislocation pile-up and work hardening.
Reduced barriers to dislocation motion promote plasticity while limiting strength.
Reduced barriers to dislocation motion promote machinability.
The starting material is as-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a homogeneous simple solid solution.
The starting material contains no pre-existing nanoscale precipitates or short-range order.
The proposed structural signature of the mechanism includes wide stacking faults.
The proposed structural signature includes rapid cross-slip and a low density of dislocation pile-ups or tangles.
Lower-SFE alloys should have greater hardness and yield strength than equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Low stacking-fault energy favors mechanical twinning, whereas high-SFE FCC materials twin less readily except under extreme conditions.
Computational modeling should predict high stacking-fault energy for equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The hypothesis is limited to unmodified equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested from 25 °C to 600 °C under quasi-static to moderately dynamic tensile or compressive loading.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the behavior to high SFE but predicts wide stacking faults as its signature; wide fault separation is ordinarily associated with lower, rather than higher, SFE.

The predicted outcome invokes comparison with intrinsically lower-SFE alloys, but the experimental design and boundary restrict testing to unmodified equimolar CoCrFeNiTi and therefore do not define the required lower-SFE control.
